mainTopic: Riverbank rules, who pays for city works, and דינא דבר מצרא: a neighbor's first right to buy bordering land.
overview: The amud opens by finishing the earlier discussion about the riverbank path used by the men who pull boats. Then comes a story: רבה בר רב נחמן had רבה בר רב הונא's trees on the riverbank cut down, and the owner's curse against whoever cut them came true. רב יהודה rules that everyone, even orphans, pays for the city wall, but רבנן do not, because their Torah protects them. For digging a well even רבנן pay, though they do not join a crowd doing the digging. רב יהודה also teaches who shares the work on a river and on rainwater drainage, and a ברייתא about gardens and courtyards supports him. שמואל and רב discuss people who grab the riverbank strip or land between brothers and partners. From there the גמרא reaches דינא דבר מצרא, the neighbor's right to buy the field next to his, learned from 'do what is right and good'. It ends with how that right works: when a קנין is needed, how prices are settled, and selling a plot in the middle of one's own land.

steps.title: Closing the reason about the boat-pullers' path
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its earlier explanation: if it were not so, the boat-pullers would not be able to walk along the bank.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if not, they would not be able to walk.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a thought from the previous discussion about the riverbank path used by the men who pull boats.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier discussion was about when trees on the riverbank must be cut to leave a path for the pullers. This last line gives the reason: if things were otherwise, the pullers could not walk there anyway. So in that situation, cutting the trees would not help them.

phrases.english: And if not, they would not be able to walk.
phrases.notes: "They" are the men pulling the boats with ropes along the riverbank, from the line just before.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the reasoning from the previous section of the daf.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: In that situation the pullers could not use the bank anyway, so the trees there do not need to be cut.

steps.title: רבה בר רב נחמן sees trees blocking the riverbank
steps.stepSummary: While traveling by boat, רבה בר רב נחמן sees a forest on the riverbank and is told it belongs to רבה בר רב הונא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב נחמן was traveling on a boat. He saw a forest standing on the riverbank and asked whose it was. They told him it belonged to רבה בר רב הונא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a story connected to the riverbank law it just discussed. This step sets the scene for what happens next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The trees stood right on the bank, in the place where a path for the boat-pullers would normally be. The owner turns out to be a well-known תלמיד חכם. That detail becomes the key to the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: a forest, a grove of trees

phrases.aramaic: רַבָּה בַּר רַב נַחְמָן הֲוָה קָא אָזֵיל בְּאַרְבָּא,
phrases.english: Rabba bar Rav Naḥman was traveling on a boat,
he saw a certain forest
that was standing on the bank of the river.
He said to them: Whose is it?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: דְּרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא.
phrases.english: They said to him: It belongs to Rabba bar Rav Huna.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּה בַּר רַב נַחְמָן הֲוָה קָא אָזֵיל בְּאַרְבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tells a story that applies the riverbank-path discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The scene is set: trees blocking the riverbank belong to רבה בר רב הונא.

steps.title: He quotes a פסוק and orders the trees cut down
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב נחמן applies a פסוק from עזרא about leaders being first to do wrong, and has the trees cut down.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: "And the hand of the princes and the rulers has been first in this faithlessness." He said to them: Cut it down! And they cut it down.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר רב נחמן is upset that a great תלמיד חכם seems to be acting wrongly. He orders the trees cut down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He uses the פסוק to say that when a leader does wrong, it is especially bad, because others learn from him. He assumes the trees were blocking the public path, so he acts right away. He does not first ask the owner.

phrases.english: He said: "And the hand of the princes and the rulers
has been first in this faithlessness."
He said to them: Cut it down! And they cut it down.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְיַד הַשָּׂרִים וְהַסְּגָנִים הָיְתָה בַּמַּעַל הַזֶּה רִאשׁוֹנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story: his reaction to learning who owns the trees.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבה בר רב נחמן viewed the trees as a wrong done by a leader and had them cut down.

steps.title: רבה בר רב הונא curses whoever cut his trees
steps.stepSummary: The owner comes, finds his trees cut, and curses the person who did it: his branches should be cut.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב הונא came and found it cut down. He said: Whoever cut it down, may his branches be cut down.
steps.whatsHappening: The owner returns, sees the damage, and curses the unknown person who cut his trees.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה בר רב הונא did not know who had cut the trees. As step 1 explained, he did not have to cut them in this case. So from his side, his property was destroyed for no good reason. "Branches" here hints at a person's children.

phrases.english: Rabba bar Rav Huna came
and found it cut down.
He said: Whoever cut it down, may his branches be cut down.
phrases.notes: "Branches" is a picture word for children, who come from a parent the way branches grow from a tree.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲתָא רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא אַשְׁכְּחֵיהּ דְּקַיִיץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The owner reacts to what was done in step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The owner curses whoever cut his trees.

steps.title: The curse comes true
steps.stepSummary: For as long as רבה בר רב הונא lived, the children of רבה בר רב נחמן did not survive.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: All the years of רבה בר רב הונא, רבה בר רב נחמן's offspring did not survive.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends by telling us that the curse came true against רבה בר רב נחמן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The curse was spoken without knowing who did the cutting, yet it still took effect. The lesson is that רבה בר רב נחמן acted too quickly. The owner was within his rights, so cutting the trees was a real wrong against him.
steps.whatToRemember: Even a great תלמיד חכם must not destroy someone's property based on a quick judgment. The owner here had the law on his side.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרִי כּוּלְּהוּ שְׁנֵי דְּרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא,
phrases.english: They said: All the years of Rabba bar Rav Huna,
offspring did not survive
for Rabba bar Rav Naḥman.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי כּוּלְּהוּ שְׁנֵי דְּרַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tells the outcome of the curse from step 4.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The curse was fulfilled: רבה בר רב נחמן's children did not survive during רבה בר רב הונא's lifetime.

steps.title: Everyone pays for the city wall, except רבנן
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה rules that everyone must pay toward building the city wall, even orphans, but רבנן do not pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: Everyone pays for building the city wall, even orphans. But רבנן do not pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new rule from רב יהודה about who must pay toward a city's shared costs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even orphans, whose money is usually carefully protected, must pay for the wall, since it protects everyone. The surprise is that תלמידי חכמים are exempt. The next step explains why.

keyTerms.meaning: building the city wall (or its gate area)

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: הַכֹּל לְאִיגְלֵי גַפָּא,
phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said: Everyone pays for building the wall,
and it is collected even from orphans,
but not from the Torah scholars.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: הַכֹּל לְאִיגְלֵי גַפָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about community expenses.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Everyone, including orphans, pays for the city wall. Torah scholars are exempt.

steps.title: Why are רבנן exempt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason that Torah scholars do not pay for the wall.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רבנן are exempt. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A wall protects everyone in the city, scholars too. So it seems strange that they would not have to pay their share.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the exemption in step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why are Torah scholars exempt from paying for the city wall?

steps.title: Torah scholars do not need the wall's protection
steps.stepSummary: רבנן do not need guarding, because their Torah protects them.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Torah scholars do not need protection.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the wall is for protection, and scholars do not need it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The merit of learning Torah guards תלמידי חכמים from harm. Since the wall gives them nothing extra, they do not have to pay for it.

phrases.english: The Torah scholars do not need protection.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Their Torah protects them, so they do not benefit from the wall.

steps.title: For digging a well, even רבנן pay
steps.stepSummary: For digging a well (or river) for drinking water, money is collected even from Torah scholars.
steps.simpleTranslation: For digging a well, money is collected even from the Torah scholars.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה adds a contrasting case: for a well, scholars must pay like everyone else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exemption only applies to protection, which scholars do not need. Water is something everyone needs, scholars included. So they must pay their share.
steps.whatToRemember: The rule follows benefit. Scholars are exempt from paying for protection, which they do not need, but not for water, which they do need.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the exemption for תלמידי חכמים is not a general free pass from community costs. It is tied to the reason behind each expense.

phrases.english: For the digging of a well,
money is collected even from the Torah scholars.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts with step 6: unlike the wall, here scholars pay.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Torah scholars must contribute to digging a well for drinking water.

steps.title: Torah scholars do not join a crowd doing the digging
steps.stepSummary: The rule that רבנן pay toward a drinking well applies only when the town hires workers. When the townspeople go out as a crowd to do the work themselves, רבנן do not join.
steps.simpleTranslation: We only said this when people do not go out as a crowd. But if they go out as a crowd, no, because Torah scholars are not the kind of people who go out in a crowd.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא puts a limit on the rule from step 9 that רבנן must chip in for a drinking well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 9 said רבנן must share in the cost of the well. Here the גמרא explains that this means paying money for hired workers. It would be beneath the dignity of a תלמיד חכם to go out and dig in public with a crowd, so in that case he is not obligated.

keyTerms.meaning: We only said this when, used to limit a rule just stated
A crowd, a group going out together to do public work
People who would go out (to do such work)

phrases.english: And we only said this
when they do not go out as a crowd.
phrases.notes: He means the townspeople hire workers with the collected money instead of digging themselves.

phrases.english: But when going out as a crowd, no,
because Torah scholars are not people who go out
in a crowd.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא דְּלָא נָפְקִי בְּכָלוֹזָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the ruling of step 9 to cases of paying money, not physical crowd labor.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבנן pay for a drinking well only when workers are hired; they do not join the townspeople in digging as a crowd.

steps.title: Who helps dig a river and who helps with rainwater
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה rules that for deepening a river, people downstream help those upstream but not the reverse; for rainwater drainage it is the opposite.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה says: For digging out a river, the lower ones help the upper ones, but the upper ones do not help the lower ones. And the reverse is true for rainwater.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה gives a new rule about sharing the work of keeping a river clear and draining rainwater.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Whoever benefits from a stretch of work must help pay for it. Downstream people need the river clear all the way down to them, so they help with the upper parts, but upstream people gain nothing from work below them. With rainwater, the water flows down and away, so the upper people need the lower channel open and must help, while the lower people do not need the upper part.
steps.confusionAlert: It can feel backwards that the lower people help the upper ones. Think of it as: you help with every stretch that the water must pass through to reach you.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda says:
For digging out a river,
the lower ones help the upper ones,
the upper ones do not help the lower ones.
And the reverse with rainwater.
phrases.notes: Here the upper ones help the lower ones, since rainwater runs down past the lower people to drain away.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the topic of Torah scholars and public works to how neighbors share upkeep of waterways.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For a river, downstream residents help upstream ones; for rainwater drainage, upstream residents help downstream ones.

steps.title: A ברייתא about gardens and courtyards supports רב יהודה
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that five gardens sharing a spring all help fix damage at the top, and five courtyards sharing a drain all help fix damage at the bottom, matching רב יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is also taught this way: Five gardens that get water from one spring, and the spring got damaged, all fix it together with the top garden. So the bottom garden ends up fixing with all of them and fixing for itself. Likewise, five courtyards that poured water into one drain, and the drain got damaged, all fix it together with the bottom courtyard. So the top courtyard ends up fixing with all of them and fixing for itself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says the same thing as רב יהודה, to show his rule is supported.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The gardens are like the river: water comes from above, so everyone helps fix the top, but the bottom garden alone pays for damage near itself. The courtyards are like rainwater: water drains downward, so everyone helps fix the bottom, but the top courtyard alone pays for damage near itself.

keyTerms.meaning: It is also taught this way in a ברייתא (support for a statement)
It turns out, the result is
Pouring out, letting water run off

steps.whatToRemember: Each person pays for every part of the waterway that serves him. Spring water flows down, so the bottom user pays the most; drainage flows down, so the top user pays the most.

phrases.english: It is also taught this way:
Five gardens that get their water
from one spring,
and the spring got damaged,
all of them fix it together with the top one.
It turns out the bottom one fixes with all of them
and also fixes by itself.
phrases.notes: If the damage is down by the bottom garden, nobody above needs that part, so it pays alone.

phrases.english: And likewise, five courtyards
that were pouring water into one drain,
and the drain got damaged,
all of them fix it together with the bottom one,
it turns out the top one fixes with all of them
and also fixes by itself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב יהודה's rule with a matching ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: רב יהודה's rule about river digging and rainwater drainage.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about five gardens sharing a spring and five courtyards sharing a drain.

steps.title: One who takes over the riverbank strip is brazen but not removed
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rules that someone who grabs the open strip along a riverbank is acting brazenly, but we do not force him off.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל says: Someone who takes possession of the riverbank strip is brazen, but we do not remove him.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל gives a new rule about a person who takes over the open land along a river.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This strip was left open for boats to load and unload, so taking it is improper behavior. But since nobody owns it, there is no legal basis to remove him.

phrases.english: Shmuel says:
Someone who takes possession
of the riverbank strip
is brazen,
but as for removing him, we do not remove him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: הַאי מַאן דְּאַחְזֵיק בְּרַקְתָּא דְנַהְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Stays with rivers but moves to a new topic: ownership of the riverbank.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Taking over the riverbank strip is improper, but the taker is not removed.

steps.title: Nowadays the taker is removed because of the Persian deeds
steps.stepSummary: Now that the Persian deeds give field owners land up to where the water reaches a horse's neck, the person who grabs the bank is removed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And nowadays, when the Persians write: Acquire for yourself up to where the water fills a horse's neck, we do remove him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא updates שמואל's rule for its own time, based on how land deeds were now written.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל's rule assumed the bank strip was ownerless. Once the government deeds gave the field owner everything up into the river, the strip belongs to him. So the person who grabbed it is taking someone else's land and must leave.

keyTerms.meaning: Acquire for yourself, wording of a deed

steps.whatToRemember: The bank strip is ownerless, so a taker stays, unless the deed gives that land to the field owner, as in the Persian deeds, and then the taker is removed.

phrases.english: And nowadays, when the Persians write in their deeds:
Acquire for yourself up to where it fills
a horse's neck with water,
phrases.notes: The deed reaches right into the river, so the bank strip is included in the owner's land.

phrases.english: we do remove him as well.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Updates שמואל's ruling: under the Persian deeds, the taker is removed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When deeds grant the field owner land up into the river, one who takes the bank strip is removed.

steps.title: Buying land between brothers or partners is brazen, but the buyer is not removed
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of רב: someone who buys land between brothers or partners is brazen, but we do not force him out.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: A person who takes hold of land between brothers or between partners is acting brazenly. But we do not remove him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling of רב about an outsider who buys a field squeezed between land owned by brothers or partners.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The brothers or partners would naturally want that field, so the outsider is spoiling things for them. רב calls him brazen, but they have no real legal claim, so בית דין does not take the land away. This follows the same pattern as שמואל's ruling about the riverbank in step 13.

keyTerms.meaning: took possession / took hold of land

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
One who takes possession of land
between brothers and between partners,
phrases.notes: Picture a field sitting in the middle of land that brothers or partners own together, and an outsider buys it.

phrases.english: is brazen.
As for removing him, we do not remove him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a parallel case to the riverbank grabber of steps 13-14: rude behavior that the court does not reverse.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Buying land between brothers or partners is brazen, but the buyer is not removed.

steps.title: רב נחמן says the buyer is removed, except when the claim is only the neighbor's right
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן disagrees: we do remove the buyer between brothers or partners. But if the only claim is the neighbor's right, we do not remove him.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב נחמן said: We even remove him. But if the claim is because of the law of the bordering neighbor, we do not remove him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן argues with רב and says בית דין does take the land away from the outsider. He then adds that a plain neighbor's claim is not strong enough to remove him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב נחמן, buying land between brothers or partners hurts them enough that the court steps in. Being a mere neighbor with a bordering field (דינא דבר מצרא) is weaker, so in that case the buyer keeps the land.

keyTerms.meaning: the law of the bordering neighbor, who gets first rights to buy the field next to his

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two cases. רב נחמן removes the buyer in the brothers/partners case, but not when the claim is only the neighbor's right.

phrases.english: And Rav Nachman said:
We even remove him.
But if it is because of the law of the bordering neighbor,
phrases.notes: A בר מצרא is someone whose field touches the field being sold. He has a claim to buy it first.

phrases.english: we do not remove him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רב's ruling in step 15 and adds a limit for the neighbor's case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The buyer between brothers or partners is removed, but not when the only claim is דינא דבר מצרא.

steps.title: נהרדעי remove the buyer even because of the neighbor's right
steps.stepSummary: נהרדעי say that even because of the neighbor's right we remove the buyer, based on the פסוק 'do what is right and good.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The scholars of נהרדעא say: Even because of the law of the bordering neighbor, we remove him, because it says: 'And you shall do what is right and good in the eyes of ה׳.'
steps.whatsHappening: נהרדעי go further than רב נחמן and say the neighbor's right is also strong enough to push out the outsider who bought the field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The source is the פסוק 'do what is right and good.' Selling to an outsider loses the seller nothing, while the neighbor gains a lot, so the right and good thing is to let the neighbor have it. This is the root of the well-known הלכה of דינא דבר מצרא.

keyTerms.meaning: the scholars of the city נהרדעא

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the main source for דינא דבר מצרא, the neighbor's first right to buy, which is practical הלכה in land sales.

phrases.english: The scholars of Neharde'a say:
Even because of the law of the bordering neighbor,
we remove him,
because it is stated:
"And you shall do what is right and good in the eyes of the Lord."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Argues with the limit at the end of רב נחמן's statement in step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Under דינא דבר מצרא the buyer is removed, based on 'וְעָשִׂיתָ הַיָּשָׁר וְהַטּוֹב.'

steps.title: If the neighbor said 'go buy it,' is a formal קנין needed?
steps.stepSummary: An outsider asked the neighbor 'shall I buy?' and the neighbor said 'go buy.' Does the outsider need a קנין from the neighbor to lock in that permission?
steps.simpleTranslation: He came and consulted with him. He said to him: Shall I go buy? And he said to him: Go buy. Must he make a קנין with him, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up a new question. If the neighbor gave the outsider permission to buy, are his words enough, or does he need a formal act of קנין to give up his right?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now that the neighbor has a real right to remove the buyer, the question is how he gives that right away. Spoken permission might not be binding without a קנין.

keyTerms.meaning: to make a קנין with him, a formal act that makes an agreement binding

phrases.english: He came and consulted with him,
phrases.notes: The outsider goes to the בר מצרא, the neighbor with first rights.

phrases.english: and said to him: Shall I go and buy?
And he said to him: Go buy.
Is it necessary to make a kinyan with him, or not?
phrases.notes: A קנין here would make the neighbor's giving up of his right final.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on נהרדעי's ruling by asking how the neighbor can give up his right.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a neighbor's spoken permission is binding without a formal קנין.

steps.title: רבינא says no קנין is needed, נהרדעי say it is
steps.stepSummary: רבינא: no קנין is needed. נהרדעי: a קנין is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: He does not need to make a קנין with him. The scholars of נהרדעא say: He does need to make a קנין with him.
steps.whatsHappening: Two opinions answer the question: רבינא says the neighbor's words are enough, and נהרדעי say a קנין is required.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבינא, saying 'go buy' clearly gives up the right. For נהרדעי, permission without a קנין can be taken back, so the neighbor can still remove the buyer.

keyTerms.meaning: an אמורא who holds that no קנין is needed here

phrases.english: Ravina said:
It is not necessary to make a kinyan with him,
The scholars of Neharde'a say:
It is necessary to make a kinyan with him.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבִינָא אָמַר: לָא צְרִיךְ לְמִיקְנֵא מִינֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives two opposite answers to the question in step 18.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבינא: no קנין needed. נהרדעי: קנין needed.

steps.title: The הלכה: a קנין is needed
steps.stepSummary: The הלכה follows נהרדעי: the outsider must make a קנין with the neighbor.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the הלכה is: He must make a קנין with him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא decides the argument and rules like נהרדעי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The neighbor's spoken 'go buy' is not enough by itself. Only a formal קנין takes away his right to remove the buyer.
steps.whatToRemember: The neighbor (בר מצרא) can remove an outside buyer. Even if he said 'go buy,' his permission only counts once a קנין is made.

phrases.english: And the halacha is:
It is necessary to make a kinyan with him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the argument from step 19 in favor of נהרדעי.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A קנין is required for the neighbor's permission to work.

steps.title: Without a קנין, rises and drops in value belong to the neighbor
steps.stepSummary: Since a קנין is needed, if none was made, the purchase counts as the neighbor's, so any change in the field's value is his.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now that you said he must make a קנין with him: if they did not make a קנין with him, the field went up or down in value in his domain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a practical result from the הלכה just decided. Without a קנין, the outsider's purchase is treated as if done for the neighbor.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the neighbor never truly gave up his right, he can still take the field by paying the buyer back. So if the price rises or falls, the gain or loss is the neighbor's.

keyTerms.meaning: went up and went down in value
in his domain, at his gain or loss

steps.whatToRemember: With no קנין, the outside buyer is treated like the neighbor's stand-in, and changes in the field's value belong to the neighbor.

phrases.english: Now that you have said
that it is necessary to make a kinyan with him,
if they did not make a kinyan with him,
it went up or down in value in his domain.
phrases.notes: "His" means the neighbor's. He gains if the price rises and loses if it drops.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a practical result from the הלכה in step 20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Without a קנין, any change in the field's value is the neighbor's gain or loss.

steps.title: The buyer got a bargain: how much does the neighbor pay?
steps.stepSummary: If the outsider bought for 100 a field worth 200, we check whether the seller sells that cheaply to everyone. If yes, the neighbor pays 100. If not, the neighbor pays 200.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he bought it for one hundred and it was worth two hundred, we look into it. If the seller sells cheaply to everyone, the neighbor gives the buyer one hundred and takes the field. If not, the neighbor gives him two hundred and takes it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא applies the rule that the purchase counts as the neighbor's to a case where the outsider got a bargain. It explains how much money the neighbor must hand over.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is who the cheap price really belongs to. If the seller sells cheaply to everyone, the neighbor could have gotten that price himself, so he pays only 100. If the discount was a personal favor to this buyer, the neighbor has no claim to it and must pay the full 200.

keyTerms.meaning: We see, we look into it
Sells cheaply, gives a low price

phrases.english: If he bought it for one hundred and it was worth two hundred,
phrases.notes: "He" is the outside buyer from the earlier steps, the one who bought before the neighbor could.

phrases.english: we see:
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets, "I see"; the corrected wording in square brackets says "we see."

phrases.english: if to everyone
he lowers the price and sells,
he gives him one hundred and takes it.
And if not,
he gives him two hundred and takes it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies step 21 (the purchase is treated as the neighbor's) to a case where the price was below market value.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A bargain goes to the neighbor only if the seller sells at that price to everyone. Otherwise the neighbor pays full market value.

steps.title: The buyer overpaid: an early assumption
steps.stepSummary: If the outsider paid 200 for a field worth 100, the חכמים first assumed the neighbor can say: I sent you to help me, not to hurt me. So he would pay only the real value.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he bought it for two hundred and it was worth one hundred, they understood that the neighbor can say to him: I sent you to benefit me, not to harm me.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now turns to the opposite case, where the buyer overpaid, and presents what the חכמים first thought. This is a first assumption that the next step will reject.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the purchase is treated as the neighbor's, the buyer looks like the neighbor's agent. An agent who overpays has gone against what he was sent to do, so the neighbor would only have to pay the real value of 100.

keyTerms.meaning: They understood from this, a first assumption that may later be rejected
To make things crooked, to harm

steps.confusionAlert: "סבור מינה" signals a first assumption, not the final law. The very next step overturns it.

phrases.english: If he bought it for two hundred and it was worth one hundred,
they understood from this
he can say to him:
phrases.notes: The neighbor is talking to the outside buyer.

phrases.english: I sent you to benefit me,
and not to harm me.

steps.triggerLanguage: זְבַן בְּמָאתַן וְשָׁוְיָא מְאָה, סְבוּר מִינָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes up the reverse of step 22: overpaying instead of getting a bargain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: First assumption: the neighbor pays only the true value, because the buyer counts as his agent who was sent to benefit him.

steps.title: No price fraud for land, so the buyer's price stands
steps.stepSummary: מר קשישא בריה דרב חסדא tells רב אשי that the נהרדעי say in the name of רב נחמן: there is no אונאה for land. So the buyer cannot be called an overpayer, and the first assumption is rejected.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר קשישא, son of רב חסדא, said to רב אשי: This is what the נהרדעי say in the name of רב נחמן: There is no price fraud for land.
steps.whatsHappening: מר קשישא pushes back on the assumption from step 23 by bringing the rule that there is no אונאה for land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The neighbor's claim, "you harmed me," depends on calling 200 an overpayment. Since there is no אונאה for land, the price paid is not treated as a mistake. So the neighbor cannot reduce what he pays and must pay what the buyer paid.

keyTerms.meaning: Mar the Elder, son of רב חסדא
Price fraud, paying too much or charging too much

steps.whatToRemember: Bargain: the neighbor pays the low price only if the seller sells that cheaply to everyone. Overpaying: the neighbor pays what the buyer paid, because there is no אונאה for land.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the general rule "אין אונאה לקרקעות" deciding a practical question in דינא דבר מצרא.

phrases.english: Mar the Elder said to him,
the son of Rav Ḥisda, to Rav Ashi:
This is what the Sages of Neharde'a say
in the name of Rav Naḥman:
There is no price fraud for land.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ מָר קַשִּׁישָׁא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב חִסְדָּא לְרַב אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the assumption of step 23.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The assumption that the neighbor can pay only the market value when the buyer overpaid.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It treats the higher price as an overpayment, but land has no אונאה, so the price paid is not considered a mistake.

steps.title: Selling a plot in the middle of one's own property
steps.stepSummary: If someone sold a plot of land in the middle of his property, we look at what kind of land it is. Whether it is the best land or the worst land, the sale is valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he sold him a בית סאה of land in the middle of his property, we see: whether it is superior land or inferior land, his sale is a valid sale.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a related case: a seller sold a plot surrounded on all sides by his own fields. The ruling is that the sale stands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the buyer is surrounded by the seller's land, so the outside neighbors' fields do not actually touch this plot. The quality of the land does not change the result, and the sale is valid.

keyTerms.meaning: A plot of land the size of a בית סאה
His sale is a valid sale

phrases.english: If he sold him a beit se'a of land
phrases.notes: A בית סאה is a standard size for a field.

phrases.english: in the middle of his property,
we see:
whether it is superior land
or whether it is inferior land,
his sale is a valid sale.

steps.triggerLanguage: זַבֵּין לֵיהּ גְּרִיוָא דְּאַרְעָא בְּמִיצְעָא נִכְסֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from how much the neighbor pays to a new case about a sale inside the seller's own land.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A plot sold in the middle of the seller's property is a valid sale, whether the land is superior or inferior.
